title: Guns vs. Butter
text:
Data Story  ·  NATO & OECD DAC  ·  Defense and Aid Spending 2014–2025

Every government faces a version of the same tradeoff: how much to spend on security at home versus stability abroad. NATO asks members to spend 2% of GDP on defense. The OECD asks donors to give 0.7% of GNI in foreign aid. Almost no country has ever met both targets simultaneously — and the gap is growing.







  2023
  
  Preliminary



1 — Absolute Spending: Defense vs. Aid

  The United States dwarfs all other donors on defense — but also on aid, until 2025.
  Toggle USA on and off to see the distribution among other allies more clearly.
  Note how Poland's defense bar surges after 2022, while its aid bar barely registers.


  Toggle USA

  USD billions. NATO defense data: NATO Defence Expenditure of NATO Countries (2014–2025),

  Countries shown are NATO members that are also OECD DAC donors.



2 — Who Meets the Targets?

  The vertical line marks NATO's 2% of GDP defense target; the horizontal line marks the 0.7% of GNI
  ODA target. The top-right quadrant — meeting both commitments — has historically been almost empty.
  Drag the year slider above to watch countries migrate across quadrants over time.


  


  Defense spending as % of GDP (NATO definition). ODA as % of GNI (OECD DAC definition,
  GNI approximated from IMF GDP estimates). Reference lines: 2% NATO target (vertical),
  0.7% ODA target (horizontal). Finland joined NATO April 2023; Sweden March 2024.




Sources: NATO Defence Expenditure of NATO Countries (2014–2025), published August 2025 (estimates for 2024–2025). OECD DAC Statistics, final 2024 release December 2025, preliminary 2025 release April 2026. GDP estimates: IMF World Economic Outlook. ODA/GNI ratios are approximated using GDP as proxy for GNI. Countries shown are NATO members that are also OECD DAC donors. Finland joined NATO April 2023; Sweden joined March 2024.

title: Aid in Depth
text:
Data Story  ·  OECD DAC  ·  Bilateral Aid Flows 2010–2025

Every dollar of foreign aid tells two stories: who gives, and who receives. This chart maps flows from the five largest donors each year to the countries that depend on that generosity most. Drag the slider to watch Ukraine’s rise from minor recipient to the world’s largest aid destination after 2022 — and to see how that shift displaced traditional recipients across Africa and South Asia.







  2023
  
  Preliminary




  Showing top 5 donors by total ODA for the selected year, flowing to top 4 recipient
  countries plus all other recipients combined. Flow widths proportional to USD billions.
  Hover over any flow for exact values. Donor ranking and recipient composition update
  dynamically as the year changes. Recipient shares are illustrative estimates based on
  OECD DAC bilateral ODA tables.




Sources: OECD DAC Statistics. Final 2024 data released December 2025; preliminary 2025 data released April 2026. Recipient country shares are illustrative estimates based on OECD DAC bilateral ODA tables and CRS project-level data.

title: The Rise and Fall of Foreign Aid
text:
Data Story  ·  OECD DAC  ·  Official Development Assistance

Foreign aid from 28 of 33 DAC member countries grew between 2019 and 2023 — then retracted sharply. In 2025, the United States cut overseas development assistance by nearly 57%, the largest single-year reduction by any donor on record.
